title: Great Basin Bristlecone Pine: Ancient Bristlecone Pines You Can Visit
meta_description: The species that holds the record for longevity. The Patriarch in California's White Mountains, and a Utah champion past 1,500 years at Cedar Breaks.
intro: Great Basin bristlecone pine holds the record for longevity, and it lasts by letting most of itself die. As the centuries go on, an old bristlecone keeps only a few strips of living bark to feed the green branches at the top, and the rest is bare wood polished by wind, ice and blown grit. Two of ours grow in California's White Mountains. The Patriarch, at about 3,440 metres in the Patriarch Grove, is called the largest bristlecone in the world by trunk volume, though no source gives its age, height or girth. The same forest holds Methuselah, dated at 4,858 years, and its oldest trees are deliberately left unmarked, so the twisted one a reader photographed near the Schulman Grove visitor centre claims no record. In Utah, on the rim of Cedar Breaks, a state champion is 8.3 metres round and only 9.8 metres tall, nearly all its growth gone into the trunk. The National Park Service says some trees in that grove are more than 1,500 years old, and nobody has published a ring count for this one.
